items.title: US Department of Labor obtains court order requiring NJ-based construction contractor to pay $2.2M in back wages, damages, penalties
items.summary: ENGLEWOOD CLIFFS, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a construction contractor to pay more than $2 million in back wages and damages to 323 construction workers.     Entered Nov. 16, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, the consent judgment resolves the department’s litigation alleging Premier Concrete Systems LLC and its owners, Peter Tiflinsky and Antonio Escada, violated overtime and recordkeeping provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.The litigation was a result of an investigation by the department’s Wage and Hour Division that found the company and its owners paid employees cash at straight-time rates for all hours worked and failed to pay them time and one-half their regular rate of pay for hours over 40 in a workweek as required by the FLSA. “Construction workers play a critical role across the country in ensuring safe and reliable structures. items.title: Proposed Information Collection: Office of Disability Employment Policy Quick Turnaround Surveys
items.summary: The Department of Labor, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance request for comment to provide the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed collections of information in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. This request helps to ensure that: requested data can be provided in the desired format; reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized; collection instruments are clearly understood; and the impact of collection requirements on respondents can be properly assessed. Currently, the Office of Disability Employment Policy, Department of Labor, ODEP is soliciting comments on the information collection for Office of Disability Employment Policy Quick Turnaround Surveys.

items.title: Clicks, Carbon, and Risk: Climate Attention, Persistent Financial Risk, and Real-Sector Activity
items.summary: Do shifts in public climate concern alter persistent financial risk and subsequently matter for real activity? We combine daily U.S. sectoral equity returns with a monthly Climate Concern Index (CCI) constructed from internet search intensity and decomposed into adverse and transition-oriented components. GARCH-MIDAS estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity: adverse climate concern raises persistent volatility in carbon-intensive Energy activities, while transition-oriented attention tends to reduce persistent volatility in regulated Utilities, with important differences across sub-sectors. We then construct a persistent-risk differential between Energy and Utilities and examine its predictive content for sectoral real activity using local projections. Innovations associated with adverse climate concern precede declines in Oil and Gas industrial production and employment over the following quarters, while comparable Utilities responses are limited. The production result is preserved when the financial predictor is reconstructed using the more closely matched Oil, Gas, Coal equity sub-sector and remains economically similar across several robustness checks. Overall, the findings establish a link between climate concern, persistent sectoral financial risk, and subsequent real-sector activity.
